title: Ozymandias

cards.story: A traveller describes a giant statue of an ancient king, now broken and lying in the empty desert.
cards.message: However powerful people think they are, their power doesn't last. Time and nature outlive everyone.
cards.why: Shelley was a radical (someone who wants big changes to society) who rejected kings and the powerful. This poem quietly mocks a tyrant.

title_note.heading: The title
title_note.text: “Ozymandias” is the Greek name for the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II. By naming the poem after a real, famous king, Shelley makes it about all-powerful rulers, not just one statue.

synopsis.setup: The poet tells us what a traveller told him about a trip to an “antique land” (an ancient country). So we hear the story second-hand.

steps.text: In the desert stand two huge stone legs. The rest of the statue's body has gone.
Nearby, the statue's broken face lies half-buried in the sand. It still has a frown and a cruel “sneer of cold command”.
The sculptor understood exactly what this king was like and carved his arrogance into the stone. The king is long dead, but the carving still shows his character.
Words on the base boast that he is “king of kings”. They tell other powerful rulers to look at his achievements and “despair”, because they'll never match him.
But there are no achievements left to see. Only empty sand, stretching as far as the eye can see.

synopsis.turn: The killer moment (line 12): “Nothing beside remains.” Straight after the boast, three blunt words show it was empty.
synopsis.ending: On the desert, not the king. Nature and time get the last word.
synopsis.tone: Calm and quietly mocking. Shelley doesn't need to attack the king; the ruins do it for him.

poem_intro: Highlighted words are the ones worth quoting in the exam.

poem_blocks.text:
I met a traveller from an antique land
Who said: Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert. Near them on the sand,
poem_blocks.note: Someone tells the poet about a trip to an ancient country. All that's left of a giant statue is two legs. “trunkless” = the body (trunk) has gone.

poem_blocks.text:
Half sunk, a shatter’d visage lies, whose frown
And wrinkled lip and sneer of cold command
poem_blocks.note: Near the legs, the broken face (“visage” = face) is half-buried. It still shows a cruel, bossy sneer. This king looked down on everyone.

poem_blocks.text:
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamp’d on these lifeless things,
The hand that mock’d them and the heart that fed;
poem_blocks.note: The sculptor “read” the king's feelings well and carved them in stone. “mock’d” means copied, and also made fun of. The art has lasted; the king hasn't.

poem_blocks.text:
And on the pedestal these words appear:
‘My name is Ozymandias, king of kings:
Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!’
poem_blocks.note: The king's boast, carved on the base, tells other rulers to look at what he built and give up, because they can never match him. Irony: there's nothing left to look at.

poem_blocks.text:
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare,
The lone and level sands stretch far away.
poem_blocks.note: Just empty desert all around the huge (“colossal”) ruin. Time and nature have beaten the “king of kings”.

quotes.why: the king is pushed far into the past.

he was a cruel, bossy ruler.

form.heading: The form: what a sonnet is, and what Shelley does with it
explain: A 14-line poem, usually in iambic pentameter: about ten syllables a line, in a da-DUM, da-DUM rhythm.
It began in Italy and was perfected by the poet Petrarch in the 14th century. Britannica; EBSCO
Traditionally used for love poems, but later poets used it for other subjects, including politics. Britannica; EBSCO politics: one source
Why poets use it: it is built like an argument. It sets up a problem, then a volta (Italian for “turn”) changes direction to answer it. Britannica; poets.org; Poetry Archive

Petrarchan (Italian): 8 lines (octave) + 6 lines (sestet); rhyme ABBAABBA, then CDECDE or similar; the turn comes between lines 8 and 9: the octave sets up a problem, the sestet answers it. Britannica; poets.org; EBSCO
Shakespearean (English): three 4-line quatrains + a 2-line couplet; rhyme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG; the final couplet often sums up or twists the argument. Britannica; poets.org; Poetry Archive
this_poem: So which type is Ozymandias? Neither: Shelley breaks the rules.
It has 14 lines of iambic pentameter, the traditional elements. Gale, Poetry for Students
But its rhyme scheme is ABABACDCEDEFEF, which matches neither type: “Rather than adhere to the English or Petrarchan rhyme schemes, Shelley does something different”. Gale; University of Toronto
There is no neat rhyming couplet at the end, so the poem refuses a tidy ending.
Its sense splits like a Petrarchan sonnet, 8 lines then 6, but the rhymes run across the split (“things” in line 7 rhymes with “kings” in line 10). EBSCO; our check
Why it matters: one critic suggests the rhyme scheme “gradually changes over time, just as the subject matter (Ozymandias's statue) does.” Gale A broken, shifting form for a broken, crumbling statue.

The turn: the octave describes the ruined statue; line 9, “And on the pedestal these words appear:”, turns to the king's own boast, and the sestet shows how hollow it is. our reading AQA's specimen mark scheme invites comments on the “use / effect of volta”.
form.say: A sentence you could use: Shelley writes a sonnet, a tightly controlled form, but breaks its rules: the rhyme scheme fits neither the Petrarchan nor the Shakespearean pattern, and there is no closing couplet. Like the statue, the form itself is half-ruined, so even the shape of the poem shows that power cannot hold together.

methods.title: Three voices, one inside another
methods.text: The poet, then the traveller, then the king's words on the stone. Each layer pushes the king further into the past.
methods.def: a story told inside another story.

methods.title: Irony
methods.text: The boast <q>“Look on my works”</q> is followed straight away by <q>“Nothing beside remains.”</q> The poem itself proves the boast wrong.
methods.def: when the result is the opposite of what someone meant or expected.

methods.title: Ending on the sand
methods.text: The last image is the desert, not the king. AQA's 2018 mark scheme suggests writing about the sand as a “metaphor for the passing of time and impermanence of human constructions” (impermanence = not lasting).
methods.def: describing one thing as if it were another.

methods.title: A sudden stop
methods.text: Line 12 breaks off after <q>“Nothing beside remains.”</q> The full stop in the middle of the line is a sudden silence straight after the king's shouting.
methods.def: a pause or break in the middle of a line of poetry.

warn: Examiners warn: don't write “he uses a sonnet because sonnets are love poems”. AQA's 2023 report says this argument goes nowhere. Link the form to the poem's meaning instead.

timeline.text: Expelled from Oxford; George III declared insane
Belzoni removes the giant Ramesses head from Egypt
Head arrives in London; Shelley moves to Italy

items.text: Born in 1792 into a rich Sussex family; his father was an MP. Went to Eton, then Oxford.
Britannica calls him the “most politically radical” of the Romantic poets: “He rejected the monarchy, religion, war, and commerce.”
Oxford expelled him in 1811 for refusing to say whether he wrote a pamphlet called The Necessity of Atheism.
He believed poets could change society. In a later essay (published 1840) he wrote: “Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world.”
He married Mary Godwin, who wrote Frankenstein (1818). He drowned off Italy in 1822, aged 29.
King George III had been declared insane in 1811, so his unpopular son ruled as Prince Regent.
Criticising the ruler was dangerous: the editors of The Examiner, the paper that printed Ozymandias, were jailed in 1813 for attacking the Prince Regent.
Napoleon, whose army had invaded Egypt in 1798, was finally defeated at Waterloo in 1815.
After the poem: at Peterloo (1819), soldiers attacked a peaceful protest in Manchester, killing about 11 people. Shelley answered with The Mask of Anarchy.

cards.title: The real king and the real statue

items.text: “Ozymandias” is the Greek name for Ramesses II, a pharaoh of Egypt in the 13th century BC.

An ancient Greek historian, Diodorus, recorded the statue's boast: “King of Kings am I, Osymandyas. If anyone would know how great I am and where I lie, let him surpass one of my works.” Shelley's line 10 echoes it.
items.src: Diodorus (University of Chicago); University of Toronto

items.text: Members of Napoleon's expedition to Egypt are said to have tried and failed to remove a huge stone bust of Ramesses; a hole in it is said to be theirs. Belzoni removed it in 1816 and it reached the British Museum in 1818, after the poem was published.
items.src: British Museum (via Google Arts & Culture); Britannica

items.text: Shelley wrote it in a friendly competition with his friend Horace Smith; both wrote a sonnet called “Ozymandias”.
It appeared in The Examiner, a radical newspaper, on 11 January 1818, under the made-up name “Glirastes”.
Shelley was a second-generation Romantic, with Keats and Byron. The Romantics valued imagination, feeling and nature.
AQA's 2023 examiners' report praised essays that saw the Romantics “as disrupters / advocates for social change”.

context.ao3: Putting it into an answer (AO3): Shelley published the poem in January 1818, when Britain was ruled by an unpopular Prince Regent and newspaper editors could be jailed for criticising him. By showing a king who called himself <q>“king of kings”</q> reduced to a broken statue, he suggests that every ruler's power will fade too.

similar: Both show human power is weaker than nature: the king's empire is now <q>“lone and level sands”</q>; the islanders are helpless as the wind <q>“strafes invisibly.”</q>
Both show confidence that turns out to be hollow: <q>“king of kings”</q> and <q>“We are prepared:”</q>
different: Speed: in Ozymandias nature wins slowly, over thousands of years. In Storm it attacks right now: “Space is a salvo,”
Voice: Ozymandias is told second-hand by a traveller, so it feels distant. Storm is spoken by a “we” living through it, so it feels close and frightening.
Ending: Shelley ends calmly mocking (“Nothing beside remains.”); Heaney ends in fear (“a huge nothing that we fear.”)

comparisons.aqa: AQA: specimen mark scheme (“despotism”); one of the two most popular partners in 2023, with London (examiners' report)
similar: Both show an arrogant ruler, proud of his status: <q>“king of kings”</q> and <q>“My gift of a nine-hundred-years-old name”</q>
Both rulers are judged through a work of art: a statue and a portrait.
Both rulers give themselves away through their own words.
different: Whose power: Ozymandias ruled a kingdom; the Duke controls one woman, and brought about her death: “I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together.”
Does the power last? Ozymandias's power has crumbled to nothing. The Duke's power is still alive: he is arranging his next marriage.
Form: a short sonnet told second-hand, against a long dramatic monologue in the Duke's own voice.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2018 mark scheme; “an excellent choice” (2021 examiners' report)
similar: Both poets attack those in power: a tyrant king, and the Church and palace.
Both show the marks power leaves behind: the <q>“sneer of cold command”</q> carved in stone, and <q>“Marks of weakness, marks of woe”</q> on people's faces.
different: Who suffers: Shelley focuses on the ruler; Blake focuses on the ordinary people who suffer: “Runs in blood down palace walls.”
Does the power last? Shelley shows power fading. Blake shows it everywhere and still crushing people: “The mind-forged manacles I hear”
Voice: second-hand and distant, against Blake's first-person “I”, walking the streets now.

exam_box.question: Compare how poets present ideas about power in ‘Ozymandias’ and in one other poem from ‘Power and conflict’. (AQA, June 2018)
exam_box.thesis: Both Shelley and Heaney show that human power is weaker than it looks, but Shelley shows it fading slowly over time, while Heaney shows nature attacking it head-on.
exam_box.para: Both poets present human power as fragile when set against nature. Shelley's ruler calls himself <q>“king of kings”</q>, yet the poem replies with the blunt sentence <q>“Nothing beside remains.”</q> His empire has become <q>“lone and level sands”</q>: nature has defeated him slowly, over thousands of years. Heaney's islanders also begin confidently, claiming <q>“We are prepared”</q>, but the storm attacks them right now. The wind <q>“strafes invisibly”</q> and <q>“Space is a salvo”</q>, military words that make nature an army they cannot fight. Where Shelley ends calmly mocking the tyrant's pride, Heaney ends in fear of <q>“a huge nothing”</q>. Together they suggest that human power, whether a king's or a community's, is weaker than it looks.
why: Opens with a clear point that answers the question about power
Short quotations from both poems, each one explained
Compares all the way through (“also”, “Where…”) and names methods
